client: I've been really struggling with my new job at the startup. The hours are insane - I'm working until 10 or 11pm most nights, and I just feel completely drained all the time. I want to do well, but I'm starting to wonder if I can actually handle this pace long-term.
therapist: It sounds like you're putting in tremendous effort at this new job while feeling increasingly exhausted. I notice you mention wanting to do well - what does "doing well" look like to you in this situation?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client:
Doing well means not making any mistakes and keeping up with everything, but honestly I don't even know if that's possible anymore. I feel like no matter how much I work, there's always more piling up and I'm constantly worried I'll miss something important. 

It's frustrating because part of me knows this standard is unrealistic, but I can't shake the fear that if I don't meet it, I'll be seen as incompetent or get fired. The anxiety keeps me working late every night, but I'm just getting more tired and less effective.
therapist: Your words and tone both show how much pressure you're putting on yourself to be perfect in an impossible situation. Let's explore this together - what evidence do you have that making a mistake would actually lead to being seen as incompetent or getting fired?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: I get what you're saying, but it's hard to shake this feeling. Last time I made a small error in a report, my boss gave me this disappointed look that still haunts me. Even though I know rationally that one mistake shouldn't define me, it feels like people are just waiting for me to slip up.
therapist: That disappointed look seems to have really stuck with you - I hear how much weight that moment carries in your mind. When you imagine your boss's reaction, what makes you think it was about your competence rather than just a natural human response to a minor error?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I keep replaying that moment in my head, and I just know my boss was disappointed in me specifically. Everyone else makes mistakes sometimes, but when I do it, it feels like proof that I'm not good enough for this job. I can't shake the feeling that they're all realizing I don't belong here.
therapist: It sounds like that one moment has become magnified in your mind as evidence of not belonging, even though you recognize others make mistakes too. What do you think it would mean about you if this job doesn't work out?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: I guess if this job doesn't work out, it would mean I'm just not cut out for this kind of work environment. I already feel like the odd one out there, and failing would confirm that I don't really fit in anywhere. But at the same time, I know that's probably too harsh - I just can't shake the feeling that everyone else has it together except me.
therapist: Your voice sounds a bit more hopeful than your words suggest, which makes me wonder if part of you recognizes that this might not be about your abilities, but rather about finding the right environment for you. What would it feel like to consider that not fitting in here doesn't mean you don't belong anywhere?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client:
I guess part of me does want to believe that, but it's hard when I've felt like an outsider in so many places. Every time I try to fit in somewhere new, that same lonely feeling creeps back in and I start thinking maybe the problem really is me. 

The idea of there being a "right environment" out there for me sounds nice, but I don't know how to find it or if it even exists. What if I keep searching and just keep feeling this way?
therapist: I hear both the longing to belong and the weariness from searching for that place where you feel at home. That pattern of feeling like an outsider must be so tiring to carry with you from place to place. What would it look like to approach finding your "right environment" with curiosity rather than as a test of your worth?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client:
I get what you're saying about curiosity, but it's hard not to take it personally when I keep feeling like I don't fit in anywhere. Every time I try to connect with people, I end up feeling like I'm failing some invisible test of being "normal" enough. 

The idea of curiosity sounds nice in theory, but when I'm actually in social situations, all I feel is this pressure to perform and this fear of being judged.
therapist: It sounds like social situations become these high-pressure performances where you're constantly monitoring yourself for any missteps. That invisible test you describe - what do you imagine the "passing grade" would look like in these situations?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: I guess a passing grade would mean no one thinks I'm awkward or boring. But honestly, I don't even know what that looks like - it's like I'm trying to read minds and predict what people want from me. The harder I try to figure it out, the more anxious I get about saying or doing the wrong thing.
therapist: You're describing this exhausting cycle of trying to anticipate what others want while feeling like you're constantly falling short. I wonder what it would be like to shift your focus from trying to read minds to simply noticing when you feel comfortable being yourself, even if just for a moment?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: That idea sounds nice in theory, but it feels impossible in practice. When I try to be myself, I immediately start worrying that I’m being too much or not enough for others. It’s like I can’t turn off that voice in my head that tells me I’m doing it wrong. Even if I notice a moment where I feel comfortable, it’s usually followed by guilt or fear that I’ll mess it up.
therapist: That critical voice in your head seems to jump in so quickly, cutting short any moments where you might feel at ease. What do you think that voice is trying to protect you from when it warns you about being "too much" or "not enough"?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: I think that voice is trying to protect me from rejection or disappointment. But it's exhausting - I can't even enjoy small wins without immediately doubting myself. Sometimes I wonder if this constant self-criticism is actually making things worse instead of protecting me.
therapist: It sounds like you're starting to recognize how this protective voice might actually be working against you. That moment of insight where you question whether the self-criticism helps or harms - what was that like for you to notice?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, very quiet, moderate-paced speech
